Lou Gehrig's farewell speech at the original Yankee Stadium. New York. July 4, 1939

He delivered this speech, often called "Baseball's Gettysburg Address", at the age of 36.

Lou Gehrig (June 19, 1903 – June 2, 1941) was an American baseball first baseman who played 17 seasons in Major League Baseball for the New York Yankees, from 1923 through 1939.

During that time he was an All-Star seven consecutive times, a Triple Crown winner once, an American League MVP twice. He set several major league records including the most career grand slams (23) (since broken by Alex Rodriguez) and most consecutive games played (2,130), a record that stood for 56 years and was long considered unbreakable until surpassed by Cal Ripken, Jr. in 1995.

Gehrig's streak ended in 1939 after he was diagnosed with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), a disorder now commonly referred to as Lou Gehrig's disease. The disease forced him to retire at age 36 and was the cause of his death two years later.

As pictured, on July 4, 1939, Gehrig delivered the speech which has been called "baseball's Gettysburg Address" to a sold-out crowd at Yankee Stadium.

The Yankees immediately retired Gehrig's uniform number "4", making him the first player in Major League Baseball history to be accorded that honor. On December 7, 1939, Gehrig was elected to the Baseball Hall of Fame in a special election related to his illness. At age 36 he was the second youngest player to be so honored.
